name: Tara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the ore hoist at Pine Deep, a large underground mine, and lead the small crew that loads the skips. A skip is the bucket that lifts broken ore up the shaft. My two-year technical diploma helps with the gear, and I can usually hear a bearing turning rough before the meter catches it. I enjoy the exact timing; I dislike the damp and the hours when a jam holds us late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, and my partner Arun and I have grown children who live elsewhere. We used most of our savings helping his mother through an illness, so less than one month of bills is left. The mine pays me at the low end for a lead because I moved to a shorter roster to care for her. Similar hoist jobs are scarce nearby, and I hope to work to about 65. I use an AI assistant now and then to explain a manual, but I check it against the machine book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the skip crew that a quicker shift report is welcome if we still check the brake by hand. I would say the small software change is worth trying, then ask for the old log to be kept during the trial. The hoist is too important for guesswork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hoist shifts look safe, but the bank balance worries me even here. Arun's part-time care work is irregular, and another family illness would empty what little we have. I would use the report helper occasionally, after checking every number against the log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hoist roster and compare the new shift report with our written log for six weeks. I'd transfer twenty-five from each pay packet into a separate emergency account. In the first year I'd ask Arun to list the care costs we may still face for his mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The work stays familiar, but an ordinary expense can still tip us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which numbers must match in the report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The brake test time, load count and any stoppage must agree with the log. If one is wrong, I mark it and tell the next operator. A tidy paragraph does not lift a load safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much room is there for saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty-five each pay packet is small enough to start without skipping groceries. I would add more only if the care bills ease. Our current reserve is too thin for grand promises.

say: I would try **quicker reports** while keeping the written brake and load log through the trial.
I would tell the crew the **hoist checks** still need a person at the machine.
think: The **hoist shifts** look safe, but care costs and irregular partner income keep our reserve thin.
I would use the **report helper** occasionally and check its figures myself.
do: Keep the **hoist roster** and compare digital reports with written logs for six weeks.
Transfer **twenty-five per payday** into an emergency account during the first year.
S0.quote: A tidy paragraph does not lift a load safely.
fieldNote: She tests **report accuracy** against three named measures before relying on it.
The **care bills** explain why a stable mine job still leaves the household uneasy.

steps.text: Keep operating the Pine Deep ore hoist on current shifts
Transfer twenty-five from each pay packet into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software may take schedules and parts orders first, not the physical lift overnight. If the mine tests remote hoists later, it should run one beside an experienced operator before cutting posts. I would ask for the test results at the safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling part of my lead role could shrink, and eventually one operator might watch more than one hoist. I might lose hours, even if the mine values my fault finding. There are few local jobs like this, and we do not have a reserve to wait out a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and ask to observe the first remote hoist trial on a paid day, if the mine schedules one. I'd bring a checklist of brake and cable faults to the safety meeting this month. In the first year I'd increase our emergency transfer by another twenty if the care bills allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A reduction in my own hours would reach the household quickly, even if the machinery changes slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for during a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how quickly someone spots a dragging brake and who can stop the lift. If the remote operator misses a fault, it goes in the record. I would judge a remote hoist trial on brake-fault detection and stopping time, not on a demonstration video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for the remote post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid course after a trial shows the system works and the mine identifies a job. I would not spend our last savings on a place that leads nowhere. I am open to the screen if it earns my trust.

say: I would ask for **remote trial results** before any hoist posts are cut.
I would tell the crew **orders and schedules** change ahead of the physical lift.
think: My **lead hours** might shrink as the mine combines hoist oversight.
Few **nearby posts** and thin savings leave little room to wait.
do: Observe a **paid remote trial** if scheduled and take fault checks to the safety meeting.
Add **twenty more** to emergency savings each pay day if care bills allow.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible cut in my own hours.
S1.quote: I would judge a remote hoist trial on brake-fault detection and stopping time, not on a demonstration video.
fieldNote: Her **test standard** is a dragging brake and a clear stop command.
Her **training interest** depends on a proven system and a real paid role.
Her **savings increase** remains conditional on the next care bills.

steps.text: Observe the first paid remote hoist trial if scheduled
Add twenty to each savings transfer if care bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could handle the lift schedule and parts list, while capable hands-on robots come around 2031 on the card. I would ask the mine for a written plan for operators at both dates. I would also ask whether safety testing will be public to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the thinking tasks change and 63 at the robot date, two years short of my hoped-for stop. A remotely operated hoist might still need my judgment, but I cannot assume the mine keeps this crew. If my wage stops, Arun's irregular pay and our tiny reserve cannot cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freeze the planned bathroom repairs now and put that money into emergency cash. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for the mine's open hoist safety role if one is posted and ask for a paid trial on the remote console if a real post is attached. I'd contact our grown daughter about temporary help only if my shifts actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect the household income could fall badly, and I would lie awake checking the dates. I have steps to take, but no guaranteed landing place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is set aside for the bathroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have about two thousand set aside for the tiles and floor. I would keep it as bill money until the mine gives us a clear roster. A bathroom can wait longer than food or the housing payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughter right away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my grown daughter Lale has her own rent and work to manage. I would tell her our position honestly, then ask for help only if we lose shifts. I will not count her wages as our plan.

say: I would separate **2028 scheduling** changes from the 2031 hands-on robot risk.
I would seek a **written operator plan** and crew access to safety results.
think: Losing my **hoist wage** around 2031 could leave us two years short of my planned stop.
Arun’s **irregular pay** and our small reserve cannot cover a long gap.
do: Postpone the **bathroom repairs** and keep their budget in emergency cash now.
Apply for a **hoist safety post** after 2028 if advertised and request a paid console trial.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely household income gap, with no assured landing place.
S2.quote: A bathroom can wait longer than food or the housing payment.
fieldNote: She treats **2028 desk work** and 2031 physical automation as separate changes.
The **repair budget** becomes immediate bill protection, with no assumed outside support.
Her **console trial** requires pay and an actual position, not an abstract course offer.

steps.text: Postpone the planned bathroom repairs this month
Apply for an advertised hoist safety role after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test a remote hoist properly and train operators before changing the crew. AGI by 2031 may handle schedules, with capable hands-on robots around 2034. I would ask for the operator jobs to be posted before the first training intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031 I would be close to 65, but a cut in lead duties could come earlier. If the remote system is proven and there is a paid post, I can learn it. If not, our savings would not carry two years without my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the next paid remote hoist course this year if the mine posts a job at the end of it. I'd keep my current shifts and add thirty each pay day to emergency savings if care bills allow. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for that posted remote role if the safety trial passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years is time to learn something tested, but a job offer still has to exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a passed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the records on brake faults, false stops and operator response times. A safety officer should sign the hoist brake-fault and response-time records, not only the sales team. Then I would sit at the console and learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another hoist job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the pay and housing costs first with Arun. There are few similar openings nearby, but moving could cost more than we gain. I would not decide from a map alone.

say: I would seek **posted remote jobs** before the mine enrolls operators in training.
I would distinguish **2031 schedules** from the hands-on robot date around 2034.
think: A **paid remote post** could bridge me toward my planned stop at 65.
Without that role, **thin savings** cannot cover two years of lost wage.
do: Enroll in a **paid remote course** this year if a job is posted at its end.
Add **thirty per payday** to savings if care bills allow and apply after a passed trial.
feel: **Anxious** because the course and safety trial do not guarantee a job.
S3.quote: A safety officer should sign the hoist brake-fault and response-time records, not only the sales team.
fieldNote: Her **course decision** depends on pay and a posted job, with safety data as another check.
She treats **relocation costs** as real, given the shortage of nearby posts.

steps.text: Enroll in paid remote training this year if a job is posted
Add thirty to each savings transfer if care bills allow
Apply for a posted remote hoist job after a passed safety trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to publish equipment plans and give the younger operators paid practice. AGI by 2036 might take schedules, and capable hands-on robots arrive around 2039 on the card. I would ask the mine to update the plan each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 at the robot date. If I work to 65, those changes come after I stop. What bothers me now is the thin reserve and whether the mine keeps my current roster until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hoist shifts and raise our emergency transfer by thirty each pay day if the care costs settle. This year I'd get a written retirement estimate and compare it with our bills with Arun. In the first year after 2036, if I am retired, I'd help younger operators read the mine's posted equipment plan at the community workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about our own money now, even though the robot date would be after my planned retirement. I would feel better once the reserve lasts more than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The written estimate and our actual bills would have to show a shortfall. I might work longer if my health and the mine allow it. I would not choose a retirement date from a guessed pension payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help younger operators with the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to read the hoist maintenance sheets, and I can explain where a new machine changes a shift. I would not pretend to know every future job. A useful workshop should start with what we can see.

say: I would request **annual plans** for equipment and paid practice as the 2036 and 2039 dates approach.
I would share **hoist experience** with younger operators while their careers still have many years ahead.
think: The **robot date** falls after my hoped-for stop at 65, if shifts and health hold.
My **thin reserve** is the nearer income risk even in this slow picture.
do: Keep **hoist shifts** and raise emergency savings by thirty per payday if care costs ease.
Get a **written retirement estimate** this year and compare it with actual bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about present money, though the technology dates leave a longer runway.
S4.quote: I would not choose a retirement date from a guessed pension payment.
fieldNote: Her **retirement timing** remains conditional on health, shifts and a written estimate.
She offers **practical mentoring** to younger workers without claiming to know future vacancies.

steps.text: Keep operating the Pine Deep hoist on current shifts
Raise emergency transfers by thirty if care costs ease

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The planning part could change at 60, and a robot shift around 63 would leave two years before I hope to stop. A published safety test, a paid remote post if it exists, and short-term help with bills if the wage goes would make a difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the new hoist when a bearing starts to fail at night. I can learn a proven console, but someone must still be responsible for stopping the lift. I want the person responsible for stopping the ore hoist named on the shift sheet.

headlineQuote: I want the person responsible for stopping the ore hoist named on the shift sheet.
portrait: **Tara Yilmaz**, 58, leads an ore hoist crew at a large underground mine and listens closely for equipment faults.
Her **shorter care roster** brings lower pay, with under one month saved, irregular partner income and few nearby hoist posts.
She uses **AI occasionally** to explain manuals, then checks them; she learns new systems after trials show they work.
Fast AGI leaves her **alarmed** over a two-year wage gap; slower dates help if paid work continues toward 65.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change schedules at 60 and threaten the hoist wage around 63, before her hoped-for stop.
whatWouldHelp: A **published safety test**, an available paid remote post and temporary bill support would help if her shifts disappear.
